candidates.statement: This guidance provides recommendations for next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based methods 15 used in nonclinical studies that will likely be needed to support initiation of clinical trials of 16 investigational human genome editing (GE) products. 2 These recommendations are in addition 17 to the nonclinical, clinical, and CMC considerations discussed in the “Guidance for Industry: 18 Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing” dated January 2024 19 (January 2024 GE Guidance) (Ref. 1 ). Clinical development programs of human GE products 20 should address both the risks associated with the gene therapy product itself as well as the 21 additional risks associated with GE, including off-target editing and unintended changes to the 22 genome for therapies targeting genetic diseases, including individualized therapies. For more 23 information on clinical study design considerations and our science-based approach weighing the 24 benefits and risks for human GE products, please refer to the January 2024 GE Guidance (Ref. 25

candidates.statement: Sponsors should use an appropriate sequencing strategy that meets the goals of the on-target and 99 off-target edit site analysis method being implemented. For example, for assessing editing at on- 100 and off-target sites that result in changes to a short stretch of DNA (e.g., ≤ 50-bp), a sequencing 101 strategy utilizing short-read sequencing-based methods may be adequate. 4 However, evaluation 102 of longer stretches of sequence for the presence of large insertions or large deletions may require 103 implementing a sequencing strategy that uses long-read sequencing-based methods that can 104 detect such changes. 5 , 6

candidates.statement: An on-target site is a specific sequence in the genome or transcriptome that is intended for 143 editing by the editor. The on-target editing rate can be determined by sequencing the on-target 144 site and evaluating the proportion of reads harboring the intended edit over total reads covering 145 the target site. The sponsor should report the on-target edit rate either as a ratio or percentage of 146 edited reads. Samples used for on- and off-target site analysis should be edited with appropriate 147 parameter(s) so that the resulting on-target editing rates are comparable to the rates proposed in 148 the final drug product. Achieving the intended rate of on-target editing likely ensures the 149 presence of the optimal level of genome editor activity in the samples. The sponsor should 150 report the on-target editing rates from the in vitro studies and may use the data to support the 151 adequacy of assays evaluating off-target editing activity (as feasible). Additionally, the sponsor 152 should use appropriate sequencing-based methods to measure and report the rates of both 153 intended and unintended edits at the on-target genomic edit site(s) in appropriate samples (see 154 section VI.A for recommendations on sample selection). Specific recommendations for 155 sequencing strategy and samples used for on-target edit profiling are provided below. 156

candidates.statement: Sponsors should use a targeted sequencing strategy that enables the measurement 160 of the rate of intended edits at on-target genomic location(s). Short-read or long- 161 read sequencing-based method(s) are recommended to assess the on-target edit 162 site if the editing modality imparts changes to a single nucleotide (e.g., a genome 163 edit replacing, deleting or inserting a single base pair) or a short stretch of 164 nucleotides (e.g., a genome edit resulting in insertion or deletion of a short stretch 165 of nucleotides). However, on-target edit site analysis using long-read sequencing- 166 based methods should be performed if the editing modality creates double strand 167 breaks and/or has the capacity to cause unintentional changes to a large stretch of 168 DNA (insertions or deletions that are >50bp to several kilobase pair long). The 169 sponsor should provide justification to support the adequacy of their sequencing 170 method used for on-target edit site analysis. 171

candidates.context: For DNA editors and epigenetic editors, an off-target edit site is any sequence in the genome 194 where editing activity was observed but was not intended. Similarly, for RNA editors, an off- 195 target edit site is any sequence in the transcriptome where an off-target editing event would 196 result in an unintended change to gene expression. These off-target edit sites harbor some degree 197 of homology or similarity when compared to the on-target edit site that is proposed for editing. 198 To facilitate reproducibility and sensitivity of assays evaluating off-target editing activity, we 205 recommend that the sponsor use appropriate NGS method(s) (see section IV for NGS 206 considerations) and use appropriate samples (see section VI.A for sample considerations) that 207 achieve the intended editing rate at on-target site(s) (see section V for on-target edit site 208 assessment), and us

candidates.statement: Off-target edit site nomination and confirmatory testing studies should be performed in 213 multiple biological replicates. Use of human cells that are either from patients, or from 214 healthy donors is recommended. If obtaining primary human cell samples is not feasible, 215 then a sponsor may consider using representative immortalized human cell lines and 216 provide scientific justification with data (as applicable) to support the adequacy of 217 sample(s) selected for the study. We recommend that sponsors use cells that are 218 representative of the target cell type that they intend to edit either ex vivo or in vivo. The 219 sample selection is further impacted by factors such as the mode of editing (in vivo or ex 220 vivo), sample availability, and the amenability of cells to in vitro culture conditions. 221

candidates.statement: Studies assessing off-target editing activity in ex vivo GE products should be 225 performed using a cell type that is identical to the cell type being edited for drug 226 product generation. Additionally, the samples used to assess off-target risk 227 should have on-target editing rates that are comparable to the rates observed in the 228 final drug product. If the GE strategy is aimed at correcting a mutation in patient 229 cells, then we recommend that sponsors use patient-derived samples or normal 230 cells that are engineered to harbor the mutation. This approach will facilitate 231 reporting of editing rates at the on-target site. The sponsor may use healthy donor 232 samples where appropriate and provide scientific justification to support the 233 adequacy of the approach. If the sponsor chooses a cell type that is different from 234 the cell type they intend to edit, they should provide scientific justification to 235 support the adequacy of their sample selection strategy. 236

candidates.statement: If an intended edit is aimed at correcting a disease-causing mutation, then the use 251 of healthy donor samples would not allow for the evaluation of on-target editing 252 rates. In such a case, using patient-derived cells or normal cells engineered to 253 harbor the target mutation is recommended for the assessment of off-target editing 254 activity. If cells harboring the target mutation cannot be used because such cells 255 are unavailable, (due to disease severity or rarity, patient cell availability, etc.,) 256 sponsors may consider using healthy donor samples and provide scientific 257 justification to support the adequacy of the approach. Finally, the data from 258 biodistribution studies, as discussed in the January 2024 GE Guidance (Ref. 1), 259 should inform the need to conduct additional on-target site analysis, off-target edit 260 site nomination, and off-target edit site confirmation analyses in other cell type(s) 261 representative of (non-target) tissues or organs where the product was detected. 262

candidates.statement: Cell-based and biochemical assays were originally developed for assessment of off-target 285 editing activity of genome editors that create double strand breaks in the genome. 286 However, these assays have been modified, or new assays have been developed, to detect 287 single strand breaks/nicks in the genome. Thus, sponsors should consider the mechanism 288 of action of their proposed editor and choose an appropriate method for off-target edit site 289 nomination. For example, assays designed to detect off-target editing activities resulting 290 in double strand breaks may not be suitable to detect single strand nicks created by base 291 editors. In such a case, sponsors may consider an appropriately designed assay using an 292 endonuclease to create double strand breaks at single strand nick sites to enable detection 293 of edit events post-sequencing. 294

Confirmatory testing 418 methods may include probe-based sequence enrichment, targeted sequence amplification, 419 and/or other equivalent methods. While performing confirmatory testing at all the 420 nominated off-target edit sites is recommended, the sponsor may select a subset of 421 nominated off-target sites for confirmatory testing and provide scientific justification to 422 support their strategy. The rationale for selecting a subset of nominated off-target edit 423 sites may include applying statistical cut-offs, editing rate cut-off, detection of off-target 424 sites in multiple samples, or other factors. However, use of stringent filtering criteria 425 should be avoided to enable evaluation of editing rate at the nominated off-target edit 426 sites. 427

candidates.statement: Analysis parameters used for off-target edit site nomination and confirmation studies are 443 specific to the experimental design and NGS method(s). For CRISPR-Cas-based editors 444 that have been shown to recognize different versions of PAM sequence for editing, off- 445 target edit site identification strategy should include different PAM versions. For 446 example, NGG is a canonical PAM sequence for spCas9, but spCas9 has been shown to 447 recognize non-canonical PAM sequences as well. The sponsor should reference peer- 448 reviewed publication(s) or data generated in-house, as applicable, to support their PAM 449 selection or exclusion strategy. For NGS data generated using either unbiased whole 450 genome/exome/transcriptome/epigenome sequencing methods or targeted sequencing 451 methods, details of the filtering parameters used for data analysis should be reported and 452 supported with scientific justification. Any additional analysis parameters that are 453 sequencing-method specific should also be reported and supported with justification. 454

CONSIDERATIONS FOR OFF-TARGET EDIT SITE ANALYSIS 513 ACCOUNTING FOR HUMAN GENETIC VARIATION 514

candidates.statement: Individual human genomes harbor several million nucleotide variations. For CRISPR-Cas-based 516 editors, some of these nucleotide variation(s) may either reduce mismatch(es) between a 517 genomic site and a gRNA or may create a PAM sequence resulting in a new genomic site that is 518 potentially amenable to editing. Similarly, for other editing modalities, a variant may reduce 519 mismatch between the target sequence and a genomic off-target edit site making it potentially 520 more amenable to recognition by sequence recognition domain of an editor. In either case, the 521 off-target editing risk will be present in individuals harboring that specific variant. An adequate 522 in silico off-target analysis method accounting for human genetic variation should enable 523 reporting of potential off-target edit sites contributed by variant(s). Specific recommendations 524 and additional considerations for this analysis are provided below. 525

candidates.statement: For genome editing modalities known to create DNA double-strand breaks and/or medium to 589 large insertions or deletions (or indels), erroneous DNA repair processes at double strand break 590 sites may result in chromosomal translocation event(s) that can impact genomic integrity of cells 591 post-genome editing. In these instances, sensitive and quantitative NGS-based assessment of 592 genomic integrity in edited cells is recommended. The sponsor may consider choosing targeted 593 sequencing and/or primer-based sequencing or other genome-wide NGS-based methods to detect 594 low frequency translocation events and report chromosomal translocation rate(s) between on- 595 target genomic site(s) where double strand break events occurred during GE. We recommend 596 that the sponsor use a sequencing strategy that is sensitive and that minimizes bias when 597 performing this type of analysis (see section IV for NGS considerations). If confirmed off-target 598 edit site(s) were reported from safety analyses of the drug product, then an additional assessment 599 to evaluate potential translocation events between on-target and off-target edit sites should be 600 performed. Please refer to section VI.A for sample selection, IV for sequencing considerations, 601 and VI.F for reporting an annotated list of sites identified from this analysis. 602
